title: Al-Inshiqaq: the book in the right hand
hook: one receives his record in his right hand and returns to his people happy (84:7–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Inshiqaq, the sky splits, and the human toiling toward his Lord. Your line was toiling toward him.

A name crackles over the loudspeaker at a graduation. A walk across the stage, a diploma placed in a hand, then the turn to scan the crowd. A mother waving. A friend yelling the name too loudly. Then the walk back to them, holding the thing, toward the ones who waited. Al-Inshiqaq shows the end of yesterday's long road as a moment much like this: a record placed in a hand, and a walk back to one's people.
screen: `YOUR NAME IS READ OUT.` → `THE WALK BACK TO YOUR PEOPLE.` → `THE BOOK IN THE RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: Verse seven: as for the one given his book in his right hand. The book, kitab, is the record of a life, everything yesterday's toil added up to. Verse eight: he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning. Verse nine: he will go back to his people, rejoicing. Then the other side. Verse ten: the one given his book from behind his back. He'll cry out for ruin. And verse thirteen adds one sharp detail: he used to be happy among his people. Both men are happy among their people, once. One in this life, carelessly. One after the reckoning, with a joy that stays. In Muslim practice the right hand is the hand for good things: eating, giving, greeting. So a record in the right hand is a good record, received with honor. And the easy reckoning? A hadith in Bukhari tells how Aisha, the Prophet's wife, asked about this very verse. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ explained that the easy reckoning is only the presentation: the record is shown, and passed. But whoever is questioned closely, line by line, is in trouble. So the easy reckoning is a kind of mercy, a record glanced at and handed back. Muslims hope for it, and some ask for it by name in their prayers. The surah doesn't say what's in the book. It already said: the toil, and where it was pointed. Today's small deeds are the ink.
screen: `THE BOOK — THE RECORD OF A LIFE.` · `AN EASY RECKONING.` · `BACK TO HIS PEOPLE, REJOICING.` · `HAPPY AMONG HIS PEOPLE, ONCE.` · then, large: `RECORD IN THE RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand open on your knee, feel its weight, and picture it holding a small book, the record of this one day so far. What's in it? Choose one good deed you could add before tonight, a kindness, a fair word, a debt paid, and close the hand gently around that choice.
Al-Inshiqaq. The splitting, Surah eighty-four, where the book comes in the right hand and its owner goes home rejoicing. Today's word.
Your line: record in the right hand. Both men were happy once; only one joy stayed. Day two hundred seven, done.

howItsDone: Muslims believe each person's deeds are recorded and the record is given on the Day of Judgment; many ask God for an easy reckoning and to receive their book in the right hand, and the right hand is used for eating, giving and greeting.

Aisha asked; the Prophet said whoever is questioned closely is in trouble (Bukhari).

fork.setup: you've been given your book in your right hand, and an easy reckoning. what does the surah say you do next?
options: go back to your people, rejoicing
read it aloud to the angels
fork.reveal: he returns to his people, rejoicing (84:9): the walk back across the stage, to the ones who waited.

original.note: Arabic: "in his right hand," from yamin, the right hand, linked with blessing, yumn (Qur'an 84:7).

trapdoor: what you thought: good people get a good report card.
what it means: the record of a life, received with honor, an easy reckoning, and a joyful homecoming to your people.
what a scholar hears: yamin, right hand, shares a root with yumn, good fortune; Bukhari 4939 has Aisha asking about 84:8, and the answer that the easy reckoning is al-'ard, the showing.

sources.ref: Qur'an 84:7–15 (the book in the right hand; behind the back; happy among his people)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4939 (Aisha asks about the easy reckoning)

notes: 84:7–9 paraphrased; not certain enough of Pickthall's exact wording.
Bukhari 4939 cited from memory (the same hadith also at 103 and 6536); confirm.
'Both men are happy among their people, once' is an interpretive reading of 84:9 and 84:13; confirm it's acceptable.
